title: Knowledge check: Arithmetic Operators

questions.prompt: For “Arithmetic Operators”, which approach best supports a reliable result?
options: Inspect assumptions, run a small example, and verify an edge case.
Trust the first output without inspecting its inputs.
Hide warnings and skip validation to make the result look clean.
Change several unrelated parts at once so the cause of any result is unclear.
questions.answer_key: Inspect assumptions, run a small example, and verify an edge case.
questions.explanation: R works naturally with vectors, so indexing and vectorized operations can transform many values without a manual loop. Reliable work makes assumptions visible and checks behavior before scaling up.

questions.prompt: Which item is explicitly listed under “Arithmetic Operators” in the source curriculum?
options: Change unrelated settings before checking the input
Assume one example proves every edge case
Skip validation when the output looks plausible
questions.explanation: The source PDF lists “Addition and Subtraction” as part of lesson 28. The lesson retains the original topic wording.

questions.prompt: When applying “Arithmetic Operators” to real work, what should you do before relying on the result?
options: Validate inputs and output shape, test a boundary case, and state limitations.
Assume missing and malformed inputs never occur.
Use the same method regardless of data type or the research question.
Remove inconvenient observations without recording the decision.
questions.answer_key: Validate inputs and output shape, test a boundary case, and state limitations.
questions.explanation: Predict the output length and selected positions, then test a value on the condition boundary. Record assumptions and known limitations instead of presenting a demonstration as proof.
